text: Three hours is a strange length for a story whose whole engine is haste. Phileas Fogg leaves London on a wager with eighty days to circle the earth, and Michael Anderson uses the running time not to compress that route but to unroll it, port by port, crowd by crowd. The recognition the film gathered in 1956 clusters in one area - color photography, color art direction, color costume - which is a fair description of what it was built to do. Verne's itinerary becomes a sequence of places worth looking at, each with its own light and its own crowd of extras, while the comedy runs the other way: Fogg declines to be impressed by any of it. Family adventure on the assumption that the world is large, photogenic, and best crossed on a schedule.

The gangster is small-time, the woman is leaving a man who deals pot, and the city around them treats corruption as ordinary weather. Louis Malle shot this in English on Canadian money, which suits a story about people living slightly to the side of the place they claim as home. Money that belongs to neither of them pushes the two together; what is genuinely at stake is the pair of self-descriptions each has been maintaining, unchallenged, for years. Malle keeps the crime plot small on purpose. The 104 minutes stay on faces, and on the distance between how these people narrate their lives and what those lives actually consist of. A Golden Lion came out of it, and the Los Angeles critics named it the best film of its year.

A man stows away for Genoa because France has stopped being a country he can stand still in. He is robbed within hours of landing. René Clément made this in 1949, in French, at a moment when both countries were short of nearly everything, and his interest is in what two people with nothing to spare still find to offer each other: Pierre, who cannot explain himself, and Marta, a working mother whose daughter Cecchina reaches him first. Cannes gave Clément its directing prize for it; the Academy honored it among films from abroad. The police are a pressure rather than a plot, and most of the ninety-five minutes are meals, rooms, staircases, and the ordinary business of a port long used to men arriving without luggage.

The reward posted for information about Frankie comes to roughly the price of two boat tickets to America. Gypo Nolan does the arithmetic. He wants out of Dublin, and he wants to take his girlfriend with him, and he drinks more than he decides. John Ford builds ninety-one minutes around the hours on either side of one transaction, placing the informing early so that everything after it is spending. Ford was working in America, which meant a Dublin made rather than found: the city narrows to a few rooms and a few streets, and every person in them is someone who might notice what a man with sudden money is doing with it. Academy recognition ran to the direction, the lead performance and the editing.

A conservative American businessman flies to Chile expecting his embassy to be useful. Costa-Gavras takes that expectation apart at the pace of a bureaucratic procedure - appointments, forms, officials who are courteous and unhelpful, and a daughter-in-law he does not much like and cannot manage without. The son vanished after a military takeover, and the trail runs back through cover-ups toward the State Department that backs the new government. Cannes gave the film the Palme d'Or. It works from what happened to Ed Horman's family, which keeps the register nearer a report than a thriller, and the tension has less to do with danger than with a man doing the slow arithmetic that ends in disbelieving his own side.

A prodigy's father and his teachers want the same thing from him, and the agreement between them is the problem. Shine follows David Helfgott through that pressure into a breakdown, then forward some years to a return to the piano, one that audiences took to more warmly than critics did. Scott Hicks made it in Australia in 1996 at a scale that stays close to hands, rooms and the repetition that playing at this level demands. At home it was named the year's best film, with awards to the leading and supporting performances and to the photography, and the National Board of Review placed it among the year's best as well. The playing carries the argument; the biography is only the occasion that lets it be heard.

Ten years is a short distance from which to stand back and look at a war. Hal Ashby set this in California in 1968 and put it before audiences in 1978, near enough that they were being asked to remember rather than to learn. The premise stays domestic: a Marine officer's wife, her husband away at the fighting, and a man she knew in high school who has come back from it paralyzed. What stands to be lost is not only a marriage but the account the country was still giving of itself. Ashby lets the situation move at conversational speed instead of dramatic speed, which is where the performances live - the Academy's acting citations went to both leads, and the Los Angeles critics called it the best picture of the year.

Japan, 1159: a samurai named Moritō pulls a woman out of an uprising and decides the rescue has made her his. Kesa is married; the fact slows him not at all. What he has to bargain with is the credit he earned in the same uprising she needed rescuing from. Teinosuke Kinugasa stages all of it inside a court where rank, allegiance and mood are legible from the cloth a person is wearing, which is why the prize the film took abroad for color costume is less a footnote than a description of method - dyed silk is where pressure becomes visible before anyone speaks. A Palme d'Or and a Golden Leopard followed abroad. Eighty-six minutes, all of it a man refusing to hear an answer he has already been given.

A sixteen-year-old has reached the ninth grade with good marks and cannot read a word. That one fact holds more than any other in the film - what the school knew, what it declined to notice, how long the arrangement stayed convenient for everyone but her. Harlem, 1987. Claireece Jones is pregnant for the second time by her absent father and keeps house for a mother whose cruelty is daily and close-range. Lee Daniels films it without ceremony, and the record around it is heavy: a grand jury prize and an audience award off the festival circuit, then Academy recognition for the lead performance, the direction, the editing and the adapted screenplay. The forward motion, though, is smaller than all of that. It is a girl being taught, late, to read.

Money is the one thing here that works reliably: it buys rooms, doctors, attention, quiet. Sebastian is a successful businessman in London, estranged from his father for years; Remy is a Montreal professor with liver cancer and a circle of friends who have been arguing with him about everything for most of their adult lives. Denys Arcand calls this a comedy and means it - much of the humor comes from the collision between people who theorized their way through life and a son who simply purchases the outcome, disrupting a public health system as he goes. Ninety-nine minutes, in French, largely conversation. Arcand had assembled the same circle in an earlier film; here they return at the point where talking stops being recreational.

Everything is measured out between two Thanksgiving dinners, and the year in between does the damage. Hannah's husband falls in love with her sister Lee; her hypochondriac ex-husband drifts back toward her sister Holly; Hannah holds the arrangement upright largely by declining to make a scene. Woody Allen keeps three households in motion across 107 minutes, and the comedy comes from how well everyone behaves while behaving badly. Academy recognition followed for picture, direction and editing, and the film sits on TSPDT's thousand-title list. But the frame does the quiet work: a year is long enough for a betrayal to settle into a fact people live with, and a table set twice says so without a line of explanation.

A life story that keeps stopping to introduce the real person it is about. Harvey Pekar is the everyman hero of comic books made out of ordinary days, which is a strange thing to be and stranger still to have filmed. The picture mixes invention with documentary rather than choosing between them, and that turns out to be the only straight way to handle a man whose existence was already split between a life and the account of it. Robert Pulcini's version is funny in a flat register that never asks for sympathy on its subject's behalf. It came out of Sundance with the dramatic grand jury prize, took best-picture votes from the Los Angeles critics and the National Society, and was named the year's best first film in New York.

Oskar Matzerath decides at three that he has seen enough of the adult world, and stops growing. He was born in 1924 in the Free City of Danzig, a place whose nationality was itself an open question, and the film keeps that coincidence in view as the 1930s close in. Volker Schlöndorff has 162 minutes and a structural problem worth the length: the grown world has to arrive at the height of a small boy, as knees, tabletops and decisions overheard from below. A Palme d'Or, an Academy award among films from outside the United States, and a place on German canon lists came of it. The comedy is real and it is not comfortable - a child's refusal to grow stays funny until 1939, when it acquires company.

Someone decided that the workhouse should sing, and 153 minutes of Dickens' London followed. Carol Reed's adaptation sends the orphan out of the parish and into a city where a gang of boys headed by the Artful Dodger picks pockets for a man named Fagin, who is at once their employer, their landlord and something close to a parent. The gang is a workforce and a household at the same time. Academy recognition ran to the photography, the costumes and the lead performance, and the BFI keeps it among a hundred British films. What holds the thing together is friction: hunger, child labor and the market price of a boy keep turning up inside the choreography, and the numbers never quite make any of that charming.
